L33: Context 1
L34: ... the implementation of the soil property content retrieval procedure, noisy or troublesome spectral bands and pixels have to be removed from the study ( Figure 1). Moreover, to isolate the bare soil areas, pixels with normalized difference vegetation index (NDVI) values over an expert-calibrated threshold were masked (NDVI > 0.20). Water areas were also masked using an expert-calibrated threshold (  smooth < 8%).
L35: Finally, 13 urban areas have been 1665 nm identified by visual inspection and have been masked. The partial least-squares regression (PLSR) method [6] was used to establish relationships between the soil property content and the VNIR/SWIR spectra. PLSR reduces the number of variables, by projecting the X-variables (the VNIR/SWIR spectra) and Y-variables (the soil property content) on latent structures, which means that the data involved are projected onto a different coordinate system.
L36: This approach seeks linear combinations of the predictors, that explain both response and predictor variation. A leave- one-out cross-validation procedure was adopted to verify the prediction capability of the PLSR model for the calibration set. Prior to quantitative statistical analysis, the reflectance was converted into “pseudo absorbance” (log [1/reflectance]), and noise reduction was achieved through a standard normal variate correction.
L37: An analysis was carried out to detect and remove outliers from the calibration set. The prediction performances of models were evaluated using the coefficient of determination R2 cal and R2 val of predicted against measured values in the calibration and validation set respectively. The root mean square errors of calibration (RMSEC) and the root mean square errors in the validation set (RMSEP) were also analyzed for all the models.
L38: The study area is located in the Cap Bon region in northern Tunisia (36°24’N to 36°53’N; 10°20’E to 10°58’E). The soil pattern of this 300 km2 area arises mainly from variations in lithology. The changes in the landscape between Miocene sandstone and marl outcrops induce large variations in the physical and chemical soil properties. And the distance between successive sandstone outcrops decreases steeply along a sea-mountain direction, which results in variations in the soil property patterns as well.
L39: On November 2, 2010, an AISA-Dual hyperspectral image was acquired for the study area with a spatial resolution of 5 m. The AISA-Dual airborne imaging spectrometer measures the at-flight radiances in 359 non-contiguous bands covering the 0.40 μm to 2.45 μm spectral domain, with 4.6 nm bandwidths between 0.40 μm and 0.97 μm and 6.5 nm bandwidths between 0.97 μm and 2.45 μm. The instantaneous field of view of the instrument is 24 degrees.
L40: The visibility was estimated of 40 km, using weather reports and visual estimations from the airplane. Moreover, the cloud cover was of 0 % during the flight-time. The United States Standard atmosphere model from MODTRAN was used. The aerosol model was taken as rural. 120 soil samples were collected on the field, over bare soils. All of the samples were composed of five sub-samples collected to a depth of 5 cm at random locations within a 10×10 m square. The studied soil property was the clay content.
L41: The determination of clay content (granulometric fraction < 2 μm) was determined according to the method NF X 31-107. The clay content of the 120 soil samples varied between 108 and 772g/kg and followed a normal distribution. A PLSR model was built from each of the images at 5m: 5m_AISA and 5m_HYPXIM . The best model was obtained from the AISA airborne image (R2 val ≈ 0.75).
L42: Nevertheless, the performance of the model obtained from the satellite simulated data at 5m is only slightly less accurate (R2 val ≈ 0.71). So the atmosphere seems to slightly impact the performances of the PLSR-based prediction models. Both PLSR models built from the spectra of the 5m_AISA and 5m_HYPXIM images were applied to the entire 5m_AISA and 5m_HYPXIM images respectively, in order to obtain predicted clay content maps (Figure 2).
L43: No significant difference can be observed on these maps by visual inspection. The same large pedological units can be identified, so same relative predictions have been made by both PLSR models. Contrasted values and soil patterns appears between the Pliocene area, located in the southeast corner of the image, and the Miocene area, covering the rest of the image. Pliocene area exhibits low and weakly variable topsoil clay contents, whereas the Miocene area shows a large range of clay content values.
L44: Variations within the Miocene area are also visible. They follow the geological pattern formed by the alternating sandstone and marl outcrops, yielding low (blue) and high (red) values of clay content, respectively (Figure 2). So when a correct compensation of the atmosphere effects was done, no differences were detected between the soil property maps retrieved from airborne imagery and the ones from spaceborne imagery.
L45: Whatever the spatial resolution from 5 to 30m, the PLSR models built from simulated-satellite images were accurate (RMSEC < 100 g/kg and R2 cal > 0.6). Only slight differences of prediction performance were observed from the validation dataset: the spatial resolution of 5, 15 and 30m gave similar performance of prediction (R2 val = 0.71 and RMSEP = 90g/kg), whereas the spatial resolution of 20m provided better performance (R2 val = 0.81 and RMSEP = 73 g/kg).
L46: The PLSR models built from simulated-satellite images at 60 and 90 m were inaccurate with R2 cal < 0.4 and RMSEC > 130 g/kg. These low performances may be due to i) the spectral heterogeneity and/or ii) the soil properties heterogeneity in the pixels of 60 and 90m. Indeed other soil properties than clay (iron, organic carbon ...) and/or heterogeneity of the land surface over the pixel (differences of ploughing, rugosity, crust...) may affect the spe ctral response and the model performances.
L47: These results indicate that the model performances do not decrease linearly with the decrease of spatial resolution as it may have been expected. Below 30 m, performances seems not be related with resolution. Conversely model performances decrease much more than linearly beyond 30 meters. Each PLSR model built from 5 to 30m was applied to its corresponding simulated-satellite image and allows obtaining predicted clay maps.
L48: As PLSR models built from simulated-satellite images at 60 and 90 m were inaccurate, no predicted clay map was built at both resolutions. Whatever the spatial resolution from 5 to 30m, no large difference occurs in absolute prediction, considering the distribution of predicted clay content over the entire area.
L49: The clay prediction map of the Kamech catchment (black upper rectangle in Figure 2) from the 5m_HYPXIM image shows a strong variation in the soil pattern on a small scale, with a close succession of clay-rich areas and clay- poor areas, oriented northwest/southeast, corresponding to marl and sandstone outcrops, respectively (Figure 3a). Some mixed areas also appear in transition areas between these outcrops and in shoal areas.
L50: The reduction in spatial resolution resulted in a decrease in the number of bare soil pixels that can be used in VNIR/SWIR spectrometry providing only a partial view of the succession of clay-rich areas and clay-poor areas. In particular, clay-rich areas with a width less than 60 m disappears when a spatial resolution of 30 m is used (Figure 3b).
L51: So although regression methods showed robust performances from 5 to 30m, the spatial aggregation of the images meant a loss of the variance of the soil property prediction from 15 m of spatial resolution and a loss of information on soil spatial structures from 30 m of spatial resolution. These preliminary works show that the use of PRISMA, EnMap, Shalom or HYPXIM data may allow for soil property mapping over large areas.
L52: A future hyperspectral spaceborne sensor with a spatial resolution at 5m would be an excellent source of data for soil mapping. Beyond 5m, the adequate spatial resolution may depend on the short-scale variability of the soil property over the study filed.
L53: As [7] showed that spatial resolution is secondary in importance to spectral resolution to map vegetation and bare soil, it would be interesting and important to engage next studies of the sensitivity of soil property prediction to degradation in spectral resolutions. Moreover, to reinforce these conclusions and the guideline, this study could be enlarge to additional soil properties.
